appraisal_events.evidence: Swann écoutait sa femme avec une complaisance, une gaieté, presque une admiration... tandis que ce que lui-même pouvait dire de fin, même de profond, était écouté par Odette... avec impatience et quelquefois contredit avec sévérité; the narrator generalizes this as 'cet asservissement de l'élite à la vulgarité'.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly frames Swann's intelligence as subordinated to Odette within the marriage: he admires her banal stories while she dismisses his finest remarks, a pattern the narrator endorses as a general rule of such households.

appraisal_events.evidence: Mme Bontemps eût souhaité qu'après elle personne de son monde à elle ne fût présenté à la princesse... Elle maudissait intérieurement le goût dépravé de Swann; in retelling the dinner she and Cottard each cast the other couple as uninvited gatecrashers ('les pelés... qui faisaient tache' / 'comme des cheveux sur la soupe').
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator ironically exposes Mme Bontemps's petty jealousy at losing exclusive access to the duchesse de Vendôme and her self-serving, competitive falsification of the dinner story, a vanity mirrored (and equally exposed) in Cottard's parallel lie and embarrassed blush when caught out.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's subtle or profound remarks are received by Odette with impatience and sometimes severe contradiction, locally weakening his rhetorical standing within the couple.
Odette's trivial talk commands Swann's near-admiring attention and her judgments override his in conversation, giving her local dominance in their domestic exchanges.
Bontemps is exposed as petty and jealous, wanting sole ownership of her new aristocratic connection and lying to friends to inflate her own standing at the Cottards' expense.
Cottard is caught in the same vanity, telling a parallel self-flattering, dismissive version of the dinner story and blushing when caught omitting the Bontemps from his account.

ambiguities: In the Bontemps/Cottard dinner episode, the narration slides into free indirect style reflecting Mme Bontemps's own perspective ('Elle maudissait intérieurement...'), so it is not fully certain how much of the diminishing judgment is the narrator's own versus a reported character perception, though the closing symmetrical mockery of both retellings reads as narrator-endorsed irony.
